title: The Horse and the Donkey

full_text:
Observing that other revered spiritual masters rode upon majestic white horses with embroidered saddles when visiting wealthy patrons, Guru Paramartha decided that his own dignity required an equine mount.

'A guru who walks on his own two feet like a common plowman,' proclaimed the Master, 'is held in light esteem. But a guru who rides a magnificent charger commands instant reverence! Go forth to the livestock fair, Matti and Madayan, and purchase for me a horse of unmatched pedigree and gentle temperament!'

The Guru handed them ten silver rupees from the ashram tin box.

Matti and Madayan hurried to the bustling town fair. Amidst the stalls of camels, goats, and cattle, they saw a cunning horse trader leading a scrawny, sway-backed, ancient gray donkey whose ears drooped like wilted plantain leaves and whose ribs looked like an upturned bamboo boat.

Matti approached the trader: 'Trader! We seek a horse for our illustrious Guru Paramartha. Does this beast belong to the noble equine race?'

The trader, recognizing the gullibility of his customers, bowed with profound reverence: 'Noble scholars! This is no common beast; this is a rare, imported Arabian steed of the royal dwarf variety! He does not grow tall because he devotes all his energy to spiritual contemplation! Notice his long, majestic ears—they are tuned to the celestial music of the spheres!'

Madayan examined the donkey's tail: 'And why does he hang his head so meekly?'

'Out of pure humility and respect for sacred philosophy!' declared the trader. 'I would not sell this celestial creature for fifty gold sovereigns, but out of devotion to your great Guru, I will surrender him for exactly ten silver rupees!'

Delighted by their extraordinary bargain, Matti and Madayan paid the ten rupees, draped a garland of marigolds around the donkey's neck, and led him triumphantly to the hermitage.

When Guru Paramartha beheld the beast, he was ecstatic: 'What a spiritual steed! Look how meekly he bows his ears! Fetch the saddle!'

The disciples threw an old wool rug across the donkey's bony back. Guru Paramartha, lifting his robes with stately grace, attempted to mount. Because of his heavy belly, it required Matti pushing from behind, Madayan pulling from the front, and Peedan lifting the Guru's left leg to hoist him into the saddle.

The instant the Guru's heavy weight settled upon the poor beast's spine, the ancient donkey groaned.

'Forward, celestial steed!' commanded the Guru, tapping the animal with his staff.

The donkey did not gallop; he did not trot. He simply lowered his head, dug his four hooves into the soft mud, and unleashed an ear-splitting, vibrating bray that rattled the tiles of the ashram roof: 'HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!'

Startled by the demonic vibration, the Guru dropped his staff. The donkey kicked up his hind hooves with surprising vigor, pitched the Guru over his ears, and sent the great master tumbling headfirst into a large heap of cow manure beside the gate!

As the disciples rushed with buckets of water to wash their fragrant preceptor, Madayan observed philosophically: 'Revered Master, the Arabian steed was merely chanting his opening prayer of reverence! Your divine ears were unaccustomed to celestial chanting!'

Spitting straw from his mouth, the Guru nodded with immense gravity: 'You speak with wisdom, Madayan. Next time, we shall ensure our ears are plugged with cotton before we ride!'
moral: A fool who mistakes an ass for a noble steed pays the price of his own credulity.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Horse and the Donkey"?
options: Foolishness of book knowledge without worldly wisdom
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
